Approved With No Questions · Everything Is On Track, Book 2

Chapter 1

About 15 minutes of reading.

The visitor badge at Marrowfield Housing Trust had been made for somebody called Gary. The receptionist peeled his name off with her thumbnail and handed the badge to Lena with the label still curled around her finger.

“Can you put Brooks on it?” Lena asked.

“Are you coming back tomorrow?”

“If I sign.”

The receptionist dropped Gary in the wastebasket and wrote BROOKS on a fresh strip. “Bring it back when you’re done on Thursday. We’re down to three clips.”

Dev Malik came out to collect her carrying a laptop against his chest and a teaspoon in his free hand. He introduced himself, looked down at the spoon and set it on the reception counter. The receptionist slid it straight back to him.

“You know where the kitchen is, Dev.”

He took Lena there first. She accepted tea and held both mugs while he washed the spoon. From the kitchen she could see the side entrance, where a woman in a raincoat was backing through the door, drawing a wheeled shopping bag after her. A man coming in behind her put his foot against the door until the bag cleared it. He waited for the woman to get her footing before he let go.

Dev had booked them a table in the room where staff ate lunch. At the far end someone had left a banana and a fork on a side plate. He turned his laptop so Lena could see the agreement.

“Thirty-eight invoices,” he said. “One batch of home modifications. Rails, steps, a few changes to door thresholds. You reconcile all of them and test twelve in depth. The fee covers all four mornings. If you finish early, you can go home.”

Lena looked at him.

“I’ve said that to contractors before,” he said. “It usually takes them a minute to laugh.”

She found the schedule. At noon on Thursday, she owed him a reconciled list and a note against each item she couldn’t clear. She read the sentence under the schedule, where the words “reasonable assistance” had survived from the template. It was easy to picture herself at the table on Thursday at twelve twenty, holding an empty mug while somebody fetched one last thing for her to look at. She took her hand off the trackpad.

“Assistance with what?”

“The list, if I need you to explain an entry.”

“Can we put that?”

Dev drew the laptop toward him. He replaced the sentence, read the new wording aloud and asked her how to spell Brooks. Then he gave her the keyboard to sign. She had gotten used to doing this on a phone while standing somewhere she needed to leave. Here the signature box was large enough for her to rest the heel of her hand on the table.

It was her second contract since she left the bank. Both had been small, with a fixed fee and an end date she could point to. These days she counted a promise in minutes before she made it.

He gave her a trust laptop and waited while she set a password. When the account opened, there were two folders on the desktop. Contractor Accounts held invoices, credit memos and the payment ledger. The authorization register was in a folder of its own.

“Anything the contractor charged, you’ll find in the first one,” he said. “What we agreed to pay for is in the register. If there’s a question about the application itself, put it on the list for me. Intake keeps the tenant files.”

“Contractor accounts and the register for me. Tenant files stay with intake.”

“Yes.”

She liked the sound of it enough to leave a little silence afterward. Dev used the silence to eat the cookie he’d brought in on his saucer.

He was due downstairs at ten. Before he left, he asked if she wanted to run one through with him there. Lena opened the first invoice. It was for a shallow step and a widened landing at a rear door. The authorization gave the dimensions in inches. The invoice gave a price for the whole job and named the carpenter who had signed it off. The two totals agreed. She entered the invoice number in her list and looked for the payment.

The ledger showed a transfer of four thousand eight hundred twenty dollars. The invoice was for six hundred ten. She clicked the transfer reference and got a scanned page with five invoice numbers down the side. Hers was the second. Someone had written a sixth number across the bottom, with sixty dollars beside it and a short pencil stroke in front.

“Is that a minus?” she asked.

Dev leaned over. “I think so. Can you make it any bigger?”

She enlarged the scan. The stroke grew into a gray blur. She could read the invoice numbers well enough to add them. With the sixty dollars deducted, they came to the amount in the ledger.

“What’s the credit against?”

He looked at his watch. “Accounts would know. Do you want me to take it?”

“Can I ask them directly?”

“Yes. Just use the contractor reference. Carol’s at the desk by the printer.”

Carol had one hand inside the printer and the other under the paper tray. Lena told her what she was looking for. Carol asked her to hold the tray. It was heavier on the left, where the paper had slipped and wedged itself under the guide. Carol freed the corner and together they got the tray out.

“Read me the number again,” Carol said, wiping a thumb on her skirt before she touched her keyboard.

Lena did. On Carol’s screen the credit showed up as a delivery charge the contractor had billed twice on an earlier job. The deduction had gone through on the next transfer. Carol opened the credit memo and showed her the posting reference.

“That’s in your folder somewhere,” she said. “Try it without the slash. They go straight through if you take out the slash.”

Back at the table Lena found the note. She linked it beside the transfer in her list and marked the step invoice paid in full. She could have written the result down before she went to see Carol and the amount would have been the same. Now she could tell Dev where the sixty dollars belonged.

A woman came in and collected the banana. She looked at the fork on the plate as though somebody else had put it there, then picked it up too. Behind her, two staff members were carrying bowls toward the microwave. Lena checked the time. She had eleven minutes left. She closed the laptop and took her mug to the kitchen so they could use the table.

Dev came through while she was rinsing it. He had his coat on and was trying to get a set of keys out of the pocket underneath it.

“How many did you get through?” he asked.

“One.”

He got the keys out. “Did it work?”

“Yes. Carol showed me where to find the credits.”

“Good. I’ll give her back her spoon.” He took it out of his jacket pocket and looked at it. “Eventually.”

At reception, Lena reached for the clip on her badge. The receptionist pointed to the name.

“You’re in tomorrow,” she said. “Keep it until Thursday.”

Lena had already unclipped it. She put it in the small inside pocket of her bag, where she could find it in the morning.

On Tuesday Carol found Lena at the shared table with a paper clip between her teeth.

“Before you start the next one, I need that sheet back.”

Lena took the clip out. “Which sheet?”

“The long one. Under your hand.”

She lifted her wrist. The contractor reference ran across the top of the page; beneath it were two sets of figures separated by a ruled line. She had clipped it behind the invoice she was checking, because the lower set of figures brought the payment to the amount she needed.

“I thought this went with the invoice.”

“It goes back to accounts. Bring it. Bring your invoice too.”

On Carol’s desk, a calculator rested across an open folder. Carol moved it onto a stack of window envelopes and drew a finger down the lower section of the page.

“Yours is here. These three above the line went through last week. They sent one total for several jobs, and the invoices came in on different days, so we split the payment.”

She showed Lena the first transfer in the ledger, then the second. Together they accounted for the contractor’s total.

“So neither invoice is the place for this,” Lena said.

“Exactly. If it’s behind yours, I look behind the first one. If it’s behind the first one, someone asks where the second payment is.”

“I should have asked.”

“You can use it. Just tell me where it’s gone.”

Carol drew the open folder toward her. A broad divider inside read BATCH SUPPORT. Behind it, sheets sat in clear sleeves with small numbered stickers at the top.

“Anything covering more than one payment goes behind here. Write the folder as well as the number. Every folder has its own numbers, so write both.”

She found the next unused sticker. Thirty-seven. She fixed it to a sleeve and slid the sheet inside.

“Until the afternoon payment run it stays on my desk. Then the cabinet behind me. Middle shelf.”

Lena wrote the folder’s label in her notebook, followed by the divider and sleeve number.

The sleeves bulged around the divider. Some held a single page; one held a folded remittance with an envelope tucked behind it. Lena could see how a short index might help. She could make one while she worked, give each shared sheet a reference, perhaps move the older batches into—

Carol lifted the calculator off the envelopes. Underneath was a handwritten list with six entries. Four had no tick beside them. Behind her elbow, another folder lay open at a payment awaiting a signature.

“For my sample,” Lena said, “will the other shared sheets be behind the same divider?”

“Yes. If it covers two payments, look here.”

“Thanks. That’s what I need.”

Carol pulled her chair in. Lena stepped back to let her sit.

At the shared table, Lena entered the two transfer references and widened the evidence column until the folder, divider and sleeve number fit. She had expected to clear four invoices by now. She had cleared two. The second had three lines of evidence instead of one.

A little before lunch she went back to accounts. Carol was away from her desk, but the folder was on the middle shelf where she had said it would be. Lena opened it to sleeve thirty-seven, read Carol’s initials and the date through the plastic, and put the folder back with its spine facing out.

On Wednesday the badge clipped to the thick part of Lena’s cardigan and pulled it out of shape. She moved it to the thin part, where it hung upside down. By the time she got to the lunchroom she had put it on her bag. BROOKS faced the leg of the table.

The first seven invoices went through before nine. She had learned to look for a slash before asking Carol for anything. On the eighth, the contractor had supplied the same photograph twice. She spent a little while looking for the difference before she realized the second picture was a close-up of the first. In the corner of both, a blue plastic peg held a net curtain away from the wet paint.

Noor Rahman’s handrail was two pages further on. The invoice specified a black steel rail fixed to the brickwork beside the front steps. It included a charge for plugging the holes left by the old fitting. Both items appeared in the authorization, down to the color. Lena followed the remittance number into the ledger. Two hundred eighty-six dollars, paid on the fourteenth, no deduction. She entered the date and amount and cleared the line.

When she went back to the register to copy the case number, she caught the corner of the cell with her cursor and highlighted the one underneath it as well. The numbers were identical. The second line was for work at a door threshold. In the status column someone had typed: estimate requested, no authorization. There was no corresponding invoice among the thirty-eight.

She searched the contractor accounts by case number, then by address. A credit for a threshold came up at a house on the same road. Different number, different name. She closed it.

Dev came in with a sheaf of paper and a mug that had left a dark ring on the top sheet. He lifted the mug, saw the ring and put it back in exactly the same place.

“Can I borrow the dry half of your table?”

“Help yourself. I’ve got a case number twice. Same household, two lines in the register.”

“Have you got two invoices?”

“One. The other line’s for the threshold. Estimate requested. Nothing authorized.”

“Then you’ve got one to reconcile.” He pulled out a chair. “If it gets authorized and somebody claims for it later, Carol will pick it up in the next batch.”

Lena took her hand off the mouse. “Does the number belong to the address or the application?”

“The application. They can come back for something else and get a new number. Or they can ask for three things at once and get one.”

He sat down and turned the damp sheet over. On the next page was a table with four rows and a total. He drew a line under one of the figures. Lena could see the row heading from her side of the table. Households served.

“Is that this batch?” she asked.

“This quarter. Your batch is the last one in it.” He moved the page so she could read it. “I’m checking that the figures survived being pasted into the board summary.”

There were thirty-one households in the bottom row. Lena had thirty-eight invoices. She had expected a difference. She had been through enough of the register to recognize addresses without recognizing what had been done at them.

“Would Rahman be in the thirty-one?”

Dev opened his laptop. He asked her for the case number and she read it out. He turned his screen toward her, keeping one hand on the base because the lid was loose. The number appeared once. The amount next to it was two hundred eighty-six dollars.

“Yes,” he said. “There she is.”

“What does served mean?”

He looked at the sheet. “On here?”

She nodded.

He opened the board pack and went to the last page, past a set of notes in type so small Lena had to lean in. He increased the zoom. Under the heading for the home modification grant was the definition the board had approved. A household entered the quarterly count when the trust recorded its first eligible payment against an application. Further payments on that application did not add to the count.

Dev scrolled a little lower to show her the date of approval. “We used to count jobs. You could put three rails in one house and report three jobs. The board wanted to know how many households the grant had reached.”

“Can I see the other numbers?”

He brought the list back. Lena ran her finger down the screen without touching it. At the bottom, two case numbers she recognized from the invoices sat one above the other. She counted the rows, lost her place where the line across the screen changed color, and started again. Thirty-one. Rahman’s number belonged there. Even if the threshold invoice arrived before the quarter closed, there would still be thirty-one.

A member of staff came in with a roll wrapped in paper, saw the two laptops and asked if they were in a meeting. Dev said no and moved his coat off a chair. The woman sat by the window and unwrapped her roll. She had brought a small knife to cut it in half. Each time she pressed down, the paper slid a little toward her.

“Does intake know whether the threshold’s been done?” Lena asked quietly.

“They might. I’d have to ask. It could be waiting for a visit, or she might have decided against it. The register would look like that either way.”

Lena looked back at the photograph attached to the handrail invoice. The contractor had stood at the bottom of the front steps. The rail went all the way to the top and bent back neatly against the brick. A brown doormat covered the join beneath the door. She had no reason to think the threshold in the register was at that door.

Dev put his hand on the board summary as if he was about to take it away, then left it there. “Do you need me to check with intake for your list?”

She considered the offer. A call would give her something else to write down. If the work had been done, she could ask when. If it hadn’t, she could ask who was waiting for whom. She could already hear herself thanking someone for taking the trouble while keeping them on the phone.

“The rail invoice is clear,” she said. “I can sign off that line.”

“Good.” He drew the page toward him. “What were you looking for in the total?”

“I was trying to see if it would tell me whether the rest of her application was finished.”

He read the heading again. The woman by the window set one half of her roll on top of the other and folded the paper over both. Dev turned his pencil around and rubbed out the line he’d drawn beneath the thirty-one. It left a shallow groove in the paper.

“The figure’s right,” he said.

“Yes.”

He gathered his pages, leaving the top one until last so he could lift it without the mug. At the door he stopped to let someone carrying two bowls pass him, then went downstairs with the pack tucked under his arm.

Lena returned to her list. She had headed the last column Status and had been typing Complete since nine. She changed the heading to Payment status. Then she went back through the rows she had cleared that morning, replacing each Complete with Paid in full. On the Rahman line, the new words took up just enough space to push the date out of sight. She widened the column until she could read both.

Thirty-eight invoices, four mornings. Now the work begins.
